topic: Principles of Holography and Diffraction: Capturing Light in 3D

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Wave Nature of Light
sections.content: Briefly review wave superposition and phase coherence. Explain that light acts as a wave (y = A sin(kx - ωt + φ)), emphasizing that interference patterns encode information about phase, not just intensity.
sections.example: Visualizing ripples in a pond merging: when two peaks meet, they create a 'super-peak' (constructive interference).

sections.title: The Mechanism of Diffraction
sections.content: Explain the Huygens-Fresnel principle. Diffraction occurs when light waves encounter an obstacle/aperture, causing them to spread. This scattering is the 'signature' of the object's geometry.
sections.example: Laser light passing through a tiny slit on a screen, creating a distinct light-and-dark fringe pattern rather than a single point.

sections.title: Recording the Hologram (The Interference Pattern)
sections.content: Show the optical setup: a laser split into a 'Reference Beam' and an 'Object Beam'. The interaction on the recording plate captures the interference fringes, which act as a complex diffraction grating.
sections.example: A 3D model of a 'Cyber-Robot' reflecting light to meet a direct reference beam, creating a chaotic-looking but highly detailed grid on the film.

sections.title: Reconstruction: Decoding the Diffraction
sections.content: Explain that when the original reference beam strikes the developed hologram, it diffracts off the recorded interference pattern, reconstructing the original wavefronts emitted by the object.
sections.example: Shining a flashlight at a flat 'Dragon Sculpture' hologram, which projects a perfect, floating 3D light-ghost of the dragon in mid-air.

sections.title: Summary and Real-World Application
sections.content: Synthesize the process: Holography is essentially 'storing diffraction patterns.' Discuss applications in secure data storage, medical imaging, and augmented reality glasses.
sections.example: Using holographic labels on credit cards to prevent forgery, where the tilt of the card reveals different diffraction depths.
